[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Self-Supervised Learning and Contrastive Learning (SimCLR, MoCo)"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Self-Supervised Learning"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in deep learning, allowing models to learn rich representations from unlabeled data. By formulating pretext tasks where the data itself provides the supervision signal, SSL bridges the gap between unsupervised and supervised learning."},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Contrastive learning is a core framework within SSL. The fundamental intuition is straightforward: pull similar (positive) instances closer in the latent space while pushing dissimilar (negative) instances apart."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"SimCLR: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"SimCLR (Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations) streamlines contrastive learning without requiring specialized architectures or memory banks. It relies on four major components:"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Stochastic data augmentation module that transforms any given data example randomly, resulting in two correlated views of the same example, denoted as x_i and x_j."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A base neural network encoder f(.) that extracts representation vectors from augmented data, such as a ResNet backbone."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A projection head g(.) that maps representations to the space where contrastive loss is applied, typically implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with non-linear activation."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A contrastive loss function, specifically the NT-Xent (Normalized Temperature-scaled Cross Entropy Loss)."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"SimCLR Loss Function Implementation"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The NT-Xent loss encourages representations of positive pairs to be close while treating all other augmented examples in the batch as negatives. Here is a PyTorch-style implementation:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def nt_xent_loss(z_i, z_j, temperature=0.5):
    batch_size = z_i.size(0)
    z = torch.cat([z_i, z_j], dim=0)
    sim = torch.mm(z, z.t().contiguous()) / temperature
    
    sim_i_j = torch.diag(sim, batch_size)
    sim_j_i = torch.diag(sim, -batch_size)
    positive_samples = torch.cat([sim_i_j, sim_j_i], dim=0)
    
    mask = torch.eye(2 * batch_size, dtype=torch.bool, device=z.device)
    sim.masked_fill_(mask, -float('inf'))
    
    loss = -positive_samples + torch.logsumexp(sim, dim=1)
    return loss.mean()"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"MoCo: Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"While SimCLR achieves high performance, it requires very large batch sizes to maintain a large pool of negative samples. MoCo (Momentum Contrast) addresses this limitation by framing contrastive learning as a dictionary look-up problem."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Dynamic Dictionary: The dictionary of negative keys is maintained as a queue, enabling a large dictionary size decoupled from the current mini-batch size."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Momentum Encoder: To prevent representation collapse caused by rapidly changing encoder parameters, the key encoder is updated as a momentum-based moving average of the query encoder."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Momentum Update Mechanism"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"The momentum update ensures consistency across the dictionary keys. The update rule for the key encoder parameters (theta_k) using the query encoder parameters (theta_q) is defined as follows:"},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"momentum = 0.999
for param_q, param_k in zip(encoder_q.parameters(), encoder_k.parameters()):
    param_k.data = param_k.data * momentum + param_q.data * (1.0 - momentum)"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion and Comparison"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"SimCLR and MoCo represent two foundational paradigms in contrastive learning. SimCLR emphasizes simplicity and strong augmentations requiring large batch sizes, whereas MoCo introduces architectural stability via momentum queues to decouple dictionary size from mini-batch constraints. Both methods have driven significant advancements in learning robust visual representations without human annotations."}]
